SEMESTER III & IV
SHORT NOTES & LONG NOTES
For use by students of Govt. T. Romana College only.

sections.title: What is an American? – J. Hector St. John de Crèvecœur

blocks.text: The essay asks what makes the new American identity. It presents America as a society formed by people from different European backgrounds and stresses opportunity, labour, social mobility and the creation of a new identity.

Crevecoeur, a French settler in New York, published 'Letters from an American Farmer' (1782); this essay is Letter III. He describes the American as 'a new man, who acts upon new principles'. Europeans of many nations - English, Scottish, Irish, Dutch, German, Swedish - mix and intermarry in America, so that 'individuals of all nations are melted into a new race of men'. This image anticipates the later idea of the 'melting pot'.

In Europe the poor were oppressed by landlords, kings and churches; in America, land is plentiful, labour is rewarded ('ubi panis ibi patria' - where there is bread, there is one's country), and the farmer owns his land. Critics note that the essay ignores slavery and Native Americans, so its picture of equality is incomplete.

The poem describes two neighbours repairing a wall between their properties. The speaker questions the need for the wall, while the neighbour repeats that good fences make good neighbours. The poem examines boundaries, tradition, communication and human relationships.

'Mending Wall' (1914) opens with 'Something there is that doesn't love a wall'. Every spring the speaker and his neighbour walk along the stone wall that separates their farms, replacing stones knocked down by frost and hunters. The speaker teasingly argues that the wall is useless: 'He is all pine and I am apple orchard. / My apple trees will never get across / And eat the cones under his pines.'

The neighbour only repeats his father's saying, 'Good fences make good neighbors', and seems to the speaker like 'an old-stone savage armed', moving 'in darkness'. Themes: boundaries between people, tradition versus questioning, isolation and community. The poem is in blank verse with a conversational tone and irony - the speaker himself initiates the yearly mending.
The poem portrays an African-American blues musician performing late at night. Hughes uses rhythm and musical language to express weariness, loneliness and the emotional power of blues culture.

Langston Hughes (1902-1967) was a leading figure of the Harlem Renaissance. In 'The Weary Blues' (1925) the speaker hears a Black pianist on Lenox Avenue, Harlem, playing 'a drowsy syncopated tune' under a pale gas light. The musician sways and sings lines such as 'Ain't got nobody in all this world' and 'I got the Weary Blues / And I can't be satisfied'.

After singing late into the night, he goes to bed and 'slept like a rock or a man that's dead'. The poem blends standard verse with blues lyrics, repetition and rhythm, celebrating African-American music while expressing loneliness, sorrow and endurance.
Ginsberg addresses America directly in a restless and critical voice. The poem questions politics, conformity, war, consumer culture and the poet's own relationship with his country.

Allen Ginsberg (1926-1997) was a leading poet of the Beat Generation. 'America' (1956) is written in long free-verse lines in a mocking, conversational tone: 'America I've given you all and now I'm nothing.' He criticises militarism and the atomic bomb ('Go fuck yourself with your atom bomb'), Cold War fear of Russia and communism, consumerism, Time magazine and media manipulation.

He mixes personal confession (his mother's communist sympathies, his own sanity) with political satire, and finally declares, 'America I'm putting my queer shoulder to the wheel', committing himself to the country despite his criticism. Themes: dissent, identity, individual freedom and the contradictions of post-war America.
Emerson argues that individuals should trust their own judgement rather than blindly follow society. He values independence, nonconformity, self-confidence and personal integrity.

Ralph Waldo Emerson (1803-1882) was the leader of Transcendentalism. 'Self-Reliance' (1841) contains famous lines such as 'Trust thyself: every heart vibrates to that iron string', 'Whoso would be a man, must be a nonconformist' and 'A foolish consistency is the hobgoblin of little minds'.

He argues that society is 'in conspiracy against the manhood of every one of its members', that people should express their own thoughts even if misunderstood ('to be great is to be misunderstood'), and that reliance on travel, imitation, property and institutions weakens the individual. Self-reliance comes from trusting the divine spark within. The essay shaped American individualism.

sections.title: I Have a Dream – Martin Luther King Jr.

blocks.text: King's speech calls for racial equality and fulfilment of the promise of freedom and justice. It uses repetition, biblical language and powerful imagery to present a vision of an America free from racial discrimination.

The speech was delivered on 28 August 1963 at the Lincoln Memorial during the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom. King begins by recalling the Emancipation Proclamation and states that a hundred years later 'the Negro still is not free'. He compares the Constitution and Declaration of Independence to a 'promissory note' that America has defaulted on, a 'bad check' marked 'insufficient funds'.

He insists on non-violence ('we must not allow our creative protest to degenerate into physical violence') and then describes his dream: that his four children 'will not be judged by the color of their skin but by the content of their character'. He ends with 'Let freedom ring' and 'Free at last!'. Devices: anaphora, metaphor, biblical and patriotic allusion. The speech helped bring the Civil Rights Act of 1964.

sections.title: The Great Gatsby – F. Scott Fitzgerald

blocks.text: The novel follows Jay Gatsby's pursuit of wealth and his dream of recovering his relationship with Daisy Buchanan. Through Nick Carraway's narration, it examines the American Dream, class, wealth, illusion, love and moral emptiness.

Published in 1925 and set in 1922 on Long Island (West Egg and East Egg) and in New York. Nick Carraway, the narrator, rents a house next to the mysterious millionaire Jay Gatsby, who throws lavish parties hoping that Daisy, Nick's cousin, will appear. Gatsby (born James Gatz, poor) loved Daisy before the war; she married the rich, brutal Tom Buchanan. Gatsby gained wealth through bootlegging.

Nick arranges their reunion. At the Plaza Hotel Tom exposes Gatsby; driving back, Daisy kills Tom's mistress Myrtle Wilson with Gatsby's car. Gatsby takes the blame; Myrtle's husband George shoots Gatsby and himself. Almost no one attends Gatsby's funeral. Symbols: the green light (Gatsby's dream), the valley of ashes (moral decay), the eyes of Doctor T.J. Eckleburg. Theme: the corruption of the American Dream in the Jazz Age.

Crèvecœur's 'What is an American?' explores the formation of a new American identity in a society shaped by immigration, work and opportunity. The essay presents the American as someone transformed by a new social environment.

Emerson's 'Self-Reliance' places the individual at the centre. He urges people to trust themselves and resist unnecessary conformity. Together, the two texts raise important questions about American identity: one looks at the making of a new society, while the other stresses independence of the individual.

Crevecoeur: The American is a 'new man' formed from many European nations, freed from feudal oppression, rewarded for labour and owning land. His identity comes from opportunity and transformation - the early 'melting pot' idea - though the essay ignores slaves and Native Americans.

Emerson: The individual must trust inner conviction, refuse conformity, avoid 'foolish consistency' and rely on the divine within rather than on society, tradition or institutions. Self-reliance is both moral and spiritual.

Comparison: Crevecoeur defines Americanness socially and economically - through land, work and mixing of peoples - while Emerson defines it inwardly, through self-trust and independence. Together they present two foundations of American identity: opportunity and individualism.

Robert Frost's 'Mending Wall' uses an ordinary rural activity to examine boundaries and inherited customs. Langston Hughes's 'The Weary Blues' brings the rhythm and emotional character of blues music into poetry and gives voice to African-American experience.

Allen Ginsberg's 'America' is openly critical and conversational. It confronts politics, social expectations and national contradictions. The three poets therefore represent very different voices within American literature.

Frost's 'Mending Wall': A conversational blank-verse poem in which the speaker questions the yearly repair of a stone wall, while his neighbour repeats 'Good fences make good neighbors'. It explores boundaries, tradition and human isolation with irony and ambiguity.

Hughes's 'The Weary Blues': It describes a Harlem pianist singing the blues, combining the rhythm and lyrics of blues music with poetry to express Black experience, loneliness and resilience. It is a key Harlem Renaissance text.

Ginsberg's 'America': In long, angry, comic lines, Ginsberg addresses America, attacking militarism, Cold War paranoia, consumerism and media while confessing personal struggles. It represents Beat Generation dissent.

Comparison: Frost uses traditional form and rural New England; Hughes uses musical rhythm and urban Black life; Ginsberg uses free verse and open protest. Together they show the diversity of American poetic voices.

Martin Luther King Jr.'s 'I Have a Dream' is a major speech of the American Civil Rights Movement. King argues that racial segregation and discrimination contradict the ideals of freedom and equality.

The speech is memorable for repetition, imagery and moral appeal. The repeated phrase 'I have a dream' turns political demands into a powerful vision of racial justice, dignity and peaceful coexistence.

Context: Delivered in 1963 at the March on Washington before about 250,000 people, the speech came at the height of the Civil Rights Movement against segregation and discrimination in the American South.

Content: King says America has given Black people a 'bad check'; he demands that the promise of liberty be honoured, warns against gradualism ('the tranquilizing drug of gradualism'), insists on non-violence and solidarity with white allies, and describes his dream of equality, brotherhood and freedom across the nation, ending with 'Let freedom ring' and 'Free at last!'.

Style and impact: Anaphora ('I have a dream', 'Let freedom ring'), metaphors, biblical allusions (Isaiah, Amos) and references to the Declaration of Independence give it moral power. It influenced the Civil Rights Act (1964) and Voting Rights Act (1965) and remains one of the greatest speeches in history.

F. Scott Fitzgerald's The Great Gatsby is set in the wealthy social world of 1920s America. Jay Gatsby builds enormous wealth partly because he hopes to recover an idealised past with Daisy Buchanan.

The novel questions the American Dream by showing the difference between material success and genuine fulfilment. Wealth, class division, illusion, love and moral carelessness are central themes. Nick Carraway's position as both participant and observer shapes the reader's view of Gatsby and the society around him.

Plot: Narrated by Nick Carraway, the novel tells how Jay Gatsby, a self-made millionaire, throws lavish parties to win back Daisy Buchanan, now married to the wealthy Tom. Their affair ends after the confrontation at the Plaza Hotel; Daisy, driving Gatsby's car, kills Myrtle Wilson, and George Wilson kills Gatsby. Tom and Daisy retreat into their money, and Nick returns to the Midwest.

Characters: Gatsby (romantic idealist with a corrupt fortune), Daisy (charming but shallow), Tom (arrogant and racist), Nick (observer, 'one of the few honest people'), Jordan Baker, Myrtle and George Wilson.

Themes and symbols: The decline of the American Dream, wealth and class (old money vs new money), illusion versus reality, moral emptiness of the Jazz Age, and the impossibility of repeating the past. Symbols include the green light, the valley of ashes and the eyes of Dr. T.J. Eckleburg. The final line - 'So we beat on, boats against the current, borne back ceaselessly into the past' - sums up its theme.
Children's literature includes texts written or adapted for young readers. It can entertain, educate, develop imagination and introduce children to values, relationships and conflicts.

Children's literature includes picture books, nursery rhymes, fairy tales, fables, fantasy, adventure stories, school and family stories and young adult novels. Its 'golden age' in Britain (about 1865-1914) produced 'Alice's Adventures in Wonderland', 'Treasure Island', 'The Jungle Book' and 'Peter Pan'.

Good children's literature uses simple yet rich language, engaging plots, relatable characters and illustrations. It develops language, imagination, empathy and values, and introduces cultures and ideas. Indian examples include the Panchatantra and the works of Ruskin Bond and Sudha Murty.
Fables are short tales, often using animals as characters, that usually communicate a moral lesson.

A fable is a short story, often with animals that speak and behave like humans, ending with an explicit moral. Aesop's Fables (ancient Greece) include 'The Tortoise and the Hare' (slow and steady wins the race) and 'The Fox and the Grapes'. India's Panchatantra (Vishnu Sharma) and Jataka tales are famous collections; La Fontaine wrote French fables.
Fables teach wisdom, prudence and moral values in a simple and memorable way.
Children's poetry often uses rhythm, rhyme, repetition, humour and imaginative language to make reading enjoyable and memorable.

Types include nursery rhymes, lullabies, nonsense verse (Edward Lear's limericks, Lewis Carroll's 'Jabberwocky'), narrative poems ('The Pied Piper of Hamelin' by Browning) and nature poems. Poets include Robert Louis Stevenson ('A Child's Garden of Verses'), A.A. Milne and Shel Silverstein.
Children's poetry develops phonological awareness, vocabulary, memory and love of language, and is often enjoyed aloud with actions.
These stories are designed to teach behaviour, values or practical lessons while entertaining the reader.

Moral tales were especially popular in the 18th and early 19th centuries (Maria Edgeworth, Thomas Day's 'Sandford and Merton'), when children's books aimed mainly to instruct. Fairy tales by Perrault, the Brothers Grimm and Hans Christian Andersen also contain moral lessons.
Modern writers prefer to teach values indirectly through character and plot rather than open preaching, balancing instruction with delight.
A school story centres on school life, friendships, teachers, discipline, competition and the experiences of young learners.

The school story began with Thomas Hughes's 'Tom Brown's School Days' (1857), set at Rugby School. Later examples include Enid Blyton's 'Malory Towers' and 'St Clare's', Frank Richards's Greyfriars stories and J.K. Rowling's 'Harry Potter' series (a school story combined with fantasy).
Themes include friendship, rivalry, honour, bullying, sports, discipline and growing up away from home.
Family stories explore relationships between children and parents, siblings and other family members.

Examples: Louisa May Alcott's 'Little Women', E. Nesbit's 'The Railway Children', Laura Ingalls Wilder's 'Little House' books and Enid Blyton's family adventures. Family stories show love, conflict, responsibility and the everyday experiences of children.
They help young readers understand relationships, cope with problems such as poverty or loss, and see their own lives reflected in literature.
Fantasy creates worlds or events beyond ordinary reality and allows children to explore imagination, wonder and symbolic meaning.

Fantasy may be set entirely in an imaginary world (Tolkien's 'The Hobbit', C.S. Lewis's Narnia) or bring magic into the real world (Barrie's 'Peter Pan', 'Harry Potter'). It uses talking animals, magic, quests and battles between good and evil.
Fantasy develops imagination and allows children to explore fears, courage and moral choices symbolically.
Adventure stories centre on danger, discovery, travel, mystery or difficult challenges and usually emphasize action.

Classic adventure stories include R.L. Stevenson's 'Treasure Island', Mark Twain's 'The Adventures of Tom Sawyer', Defoe's 'Robinson Crusoe' and Enid Blyton's Famous Five series. They feature journeys, treasure, mysteries, villains and brave young heroes.
Adventure stories build excitement and encourage courage, resourcefulness, teamwork and independence.

sections.title: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland – Lewis Carroll

blocks.text: Alice enters a strange world where normal rules of language, size, logic and behaviour are constantly changed. The novel uses fantasy, nonsense and humour to explore childhood, identity and the strange logic of the adult world.

Published in 1865 by Lewis Carroll (Charles Lutwidge Dodgson), the story was first told to Alice Liddell and her sisters on a boat trip. Alice follows the White Rabbit down a rabbit hole, drinks from a bottle labelled 'Drink Me' and eats cake that makes her shrink and grow. She swims in a pool of her own tears and meets the Caterpillar, the Duchess, the grinning Cheshire Cat, the Mad Hatter and March Hare at a mad tea-party, and the Queen of Hearts who shouts 'Off with their heads!'.

At the trial of the Knave of Hearts, Alice grows large, declares 'You're nothing but a pack of cards!', and wakes up. The book uses nonsense, wordplay, parody of moral poems and illogical situations to mock adult rules and explore a child's search for identity ('Who in the world am I?').

sections.title: Five on a Treasure Island – Enid Blyton

blocks.text: The story introduces the Famous Five and centres on friendship, exploration, mystery and adventure around Kirrin Island. The young characters use courage and cooperation to face danger and solve problems.

'Five on a Treasure Island' (1942) is the first Famous Five book. Julian, Dick and Anne spend a holiday at Kirrin Cottage with their cousin Georgina, a tomboy who insists on being called George, and her dog Timmy. George owns Kirrin Island, which has a ruined castle.

After a storm reveals an old shipwreck, the children find a map showing gold ingots hidden in the castle dungeons. Crooks try to buy the island; the children are trapped but outwit them, and the gold is recovered, saving George's family from financial trouble. Themes: friendship, courage, independence, adventure and outdoor life.

sections.title: The Little Prince – Antoine de Saint-Exupéry

blocks.text: A pilot meets a mysterious young prince from another planet. Through the prince's travels and encounters, the story explores friendship, love, loneliness, responsibility and the difference between childlike understanding and adult values.

Published in 1943, the book is narrated by a pilot who crashes in the Sahara. The little prince comes from Asteroid B-612, where he cared for a proud rose and cleaned volcanoes. On his journey he visits planets inhabited by a king, a conceited man, a drunkard, a businessman, a lamplighter and a geographer, each showing the foolishness of adults.

On Earth he meets a fox who teaches him: 'One sees clearly only with the heart. What is essential is invisible to the eye' and 'You become responsible, forever, for what you have tamed.' He realises his rose is unique because of the love he gave her. He returns home through the bite of a snake. Themes: love, friendship, loss, responsibility and the wisdom of childhood.

sections.title: Nature and Forms of Children's Literature

blocks.text:
Children's literature provides stories and poems suited to young readers while dealing with important experiences and values. Fables and moral tales often teach lessons directly. Poetry uses rhythm and imagination, while school and family stories present familiar social worlds.

Fantasy allows impossible events and imaginative worlds, whereas adventure stories focus on action, discovery and challenge. These forms show that children's literature can educate without losing enjoyment.

Nature and purpose: Children's literature is written for or enjoyed by children, with suitable language, themes and illustrations. It entertains, educates, develops imagination, empathy and language, and transmits cultural values.

Forms: Fables (Aesop, Panchatantra) and moral tales teach lessons; poetry (nursery rhymes, nonsense verse) delights through sound; school stories (Tom Brown, Malory Towers) and family stories (Little Women, The Railway Children) reflect familiar life; fantasy (Alice, Narnia, Harry Potter) explores imaginary worlds; adventure stories (Treasure Island, Famous Five) emphasise action and courage.

Development: Early children's books were mainly instructive; from the mid-19th century, writers like Carroll emphasised delight and imagination. Today children's literature is a serious literary field addressing identity, diversity and social issues.

Lewis Carroll's Alice's Adventures in Wonderland follows Alice into a fantastic world populated by unusual characters and constantly changing rules. Events often challenge ordinary logic and language.

The story can be enjoyed as fantasy and nonsense, but it also explores identity, growing up and the confusing rules imposed by adults. Alice's attempts to understand Wonderland reflect a child's effort to make sense of an unpredictable world.

Plot: Alice falls down a rabbit hole into Wonderland, changes size repeatedly, and meets strange creatures - the White Rabbit, the Caterpillar, the Duchess, the Cheshire Cat, the Mad Hatter, the March Hare and the Queen of Hearts. The story ends with a chaotic trial, after which Alice wakes from her dream.

Themes: Identity and growing up (her changing size and confusion), the absurdity of adult rules and authority, logic and nonsense, curiosity, and the contrast between childhood imagination and the adult world.

Style: Carroll uses wordplay, puns, parodies of Victorian moral poems, logical paradoxes and episodic structure. The book broke from moral instruction in children's literature and is considered the beginning of its golden age.

Enid Blyton's Five on a Treasure Island is an adventure story centred on Julian, Dick, Anne, George and Timmy. Their holiday becomes an exciting investigation involving Kirrin Island, hidden secrets and danger.

The novel emphasizes friendship, courage, independence, teamwork and curiosity. Its quick action and mystery are important features of children's adventure fiction.

Plot: Julian, Dick and Anne meet their cousin George and her dog Timmy at Kirrin. On George's island they explore a ruined castle and a shipwreck, find a map of hidden gold, and are threatened by crooks who want the island. The children cleverly trap the villains, the police are called, and the gold makes George's family secure.
Characters: George (brave, independent tomboy), Julian (responsible leader), Dick (cheerful), Anne (gentle, domestic) and Timmy (loyal dog).

Themes and appeal: Friendship, teamwork, courage, independence from adults, love of nature and adventure. Blyton's simple language, fast plot, picnics and mystery made the series hugely popular, though critics point to stereotyped gender roles (except George).

Antoine de Saint-Exupéry's The Little Prince combines fantasy with philosophical reflection. The Little Prince travels from his small planet and meets adults whose behaviour represents different human weaknesses.

His relationship with the rose and his meeting with the fox develop the themes of love, friendship and responsibility. The book contrasts the simplicity and insight of children with the narrow priorities of adults.

Plot: A pilot stranded in the Sahara meets the little prince, who describes his tiny planet, his beloved rose and his journey through planets of foolish adults. On Earth, the fox teaches him about taming and friendship. He returns to his planet through a snake's bite, leaving the pilot sad but changed.

Themes: The narrow-mindedness of adults (obsession with power, vanity, numbers and rules), the importance of love and responsibility, the value of relationships, loneliness, and seeing with the heart.
Style: Simple language, watercolour illustrations by the author and symbolic characters make it suitable for children while giving deep philosophical meaning for adults.

sections.title: ENG 202 – CONTEMPORARY SHORT STORIES FROM MIZORAM
SHORT NOTES
context: ENG 202 – CONTEMPORARY SHORT STORIES FROM MIZORAM

sections.title: Course Focus
context: ENG 202 – CONTEMPORARY SHORT STORIES FROM MIZORAM

blocks.text: The paper introduces contemporary writing from Mizoram and studies Mizo culture and ethos through the attitudes, experiences and aspirations of characters in selected stories.

Mizo literature in English is relatively recent; much creative writing is in Mizo (Duhlian). Translation and anthologies like this one bring Mizo voices to wider readers. Themes in contemporary Mizo writing often include community life and the value of tlawmngaihna, Christianity and changing traditions, rural and urban change, insurgency and peace, love and family.
When studying, link the characters' attitudes and choices to Mizo cultural values, social customs and the historical experience of Mizoram.

sections.title: That One Time – Vanneihtluanga
context: ENG 202 – CONTEMPORARY SHORT STORIES FROM MIZORAM

blocks.text: This is the Unit I prescribed story in Contemporary Short Stories from Mizoram, edited by Margaret Ch. Zama. Students should study its plot, characters, setting, themes and representation of contemporary Mizo society from the prescribed anthology.

Study plan: write a sequence of the main events in your own words; list the characters and how they change; note the setting (village or town, time period) and what it shows about Mizo life; identify the central theme and the significance of the title 'That One Time'.
Also note the narrator's point of view, the tone (humorous, nostalgic, tragic) and any cultural practices or values shown. Confirm details from the prescribed anthology edited by Margaret Ch. Zama.

sections.title: Life – A Flower – Lalrammawia Ngente
context: ENG 202 – CONTEMPORARY SHORT STORIES FROM MIZORAM

blocks.text: This is the Unit II prescribed story. The syllabus identifies it as a text through which contemporary Mizo society and cultural experience are to be studied. Detailed story content should be taken from the prescribed anthology.

Study plan: prepare a summary of the story from the anthology, the main characters and their relationships, and the key incidents. Consider how the title's image of life as a flower (beauty, growth, fragility) is developed in the story.
Examine what the story shows about Mizo society - family, community, faith, values and aspirations - and how the author uses language and symbols.

sections.title: The Haunted House – Mafaa Hauhnar
context: ENG 202 – CONTEMPORARY SHORT STORIES FROM MIZORAM

blocks.text: This is the Unit III prescribed story. Students should focus on its narrative, characters, atmosphere, themes and cultural setting from the prescribed anthology.

Study plan: note how the author builds atmosphere and suspense, the role of the house itself, the characters' reactions and beliefs, and the ending. Consider whether the 'haunting' is literal, psychological or symbolic in the text.
Relate the story to Mizo traditional beliefs, oral storytelling and community life, as presented in the prescribed text.

sections.title: LONG NOTES
context: ENG 202 – CONTEMPORARY SHORT STORIES FROM MIZORAM

sections.title: Contemporary Short Stories from Mizoram
context: ENG 202 – CONTEMPORARY SHORT STORIES FROM MIZORAM

blocks.text:
The syllabus states that this course is intended to introduce students to contemporary writings from Mizoram and to give insight into Mizo culture and ethos as expressed through literary characters. Its prescribed text is Contemporary Short Stories from Mizoram, edited by Margaret Ch. Zama and published by Sahitya Akademi in 2017.

The three prescribed stories are Vanneihtluanga's 'That One Time', Lalrammawia Ngente's 'Life – A Flower', and Mafaa Hauhnar's 'The Haunted House'. Since the uploaded syllabus provides titles but not the stories themselves, plot-specific notes should be prepared from the prescribed anthology rather than invented.

The anthology: 'Contemporary Short Stories from Mizoram', edited by Margaret Ch. Zama (Sahitya Akademi, 2017), presents translated stories by Mizo writers, giving readers access to modern Mizo fiction.

Course aim: Through the characters' attitudes, experiences and aspirations, the stories reveal Mizo culture and ethos - community spirit, tlawmngaihna, Christianity alongside older traditions, and the changes brought by modernisation and history.

Approach: Treat each story as a window into society. For long answers, combine plot summary with analysis of characters, themes, setting and cultural values, and compare the three stories where suitable.

sections.title: How to Study the Three Prescribed Stories
context: ENG 202 – CONTEMPORARY SHORT STORIES FROM MIZORAM

blocks.text:
For each story, students should prepare the plot in sequence, major and minor characters, setting, central themes, important incidents, narrative style and the picture of Mizo society presented in the text.

Special attention should be given to the course objective: how culture, social values, attitudes and aspirations appear through the characters. This gives students a reliable structure for both short-note and long-answer questions.
Step 1 - Read: Read each story fully from the prescribed anthology and note the main events in order.
Step 2 - Analyse: For each story prepare notes on characters (traits, change), setting, central themes, narrative point of view, tone, symbols and the meaning of the title.

Step 3 - Connect to culture: Identify how Mizo customs, beliefs, family and community life, values and aspirations appear in the characters. Then compare the three stories - for example, how they depict tradition and change - and support every point with incidents from the texts.
Travel writing records and interprets journeys, places and encounters. It can combine autobiography, history, geography, ethnography, politics and cultural observation.

Travel writing includes journals, letters, memoirs, guidebooks, essays and travelogues. Classic examples include Marco Polo's travels, Ibn Battuta's 'Rihla', Mark Twain's 'The Innocents Abroad' and V.S. Naipaul's 'An Area of Darkness'.

Critics like Edward Said ('Orientalism') and Mary Louise Pratt ('Imperial Eyes') showed that travel writing often reflected colonial power, presenting other cultures as exotic or inferior. Modern travel writing is more self-reflexive and attentive to the people being described.

sections.title: The Cambridge Introduction to Travel Writing – Tim Youngs

blocks.text: The prescribed background introduces travel writing as a broad literary field. Travel accounts do not merely describe places; they also reveal the traveller's assumptions and ways of seeing other cultures.

Tim Youngs's 'The Cambridge Introduction to Travel Writing' (2013) defines travel writing as 'predominantly factual, first-person prose accounts of travels that have been undertaken by the author-narrator'. It traces the history of the form from medieval pilgrimage and exploration narratives to colonial and modern writing.

Youngs discusses issues such as the relationship between fact and fiction, the traveller's identity (gender, class, race), the representation of 'others', and postcolonial and contemporary travel writing.

Ghosh's essay connects travel, memory, culture and the violent history of Cambodia. His writing moves beyond tourist description and reflects on history, politics and the survival of cultural traditions.

In 'Dancing in Cambodia' (1993), Amitav Ghosh connects two moments. In 1906 King Sisowath of Cambodia travelled to France with his royal dance troupe for the Colonial Exhibition in Marseilles, where the dancers fascinated Europeans, including the sculptor Rodin, who drew them.

Ghosh then describes Cambodia after the Khmer Rouge regime of Pol Pot (1975-79), which killed most of the classical dancers and musicians. He meets survivors who struggled to revive the dance. The essay shows how art and culture survive colonialism, war and genocide, and how travel writing can combine history, reportage and reflection.

sections.title: A Fly on the Wheel – Lt. Col. Thomas Lewin

blocks.text: The syllabus prescribes Chapters IX, X and XI from Lewin's account. These selections should be read as a colonial-era travel and administrative narrative, paying attention to the traveller's observations and the viewpoint from which local people and places are described.

Thomas Herbert Lewin (1839-1916) served as a British officer and administrator in the Chittagong Hill Tracts and played a role in the Lushai Expedition of 1871-72. His memoir 'A Fly on the Wheel, or How I Helped to Govern India' (1885) describes his experiences among the hill peoples, including the Lushais (Mizos), by whom he was called 'Thangliana'.

Read the prescribed chapters for his descriptions of people, places and events, but also critically: notice the colonial attitudes, how Lewin represents the hill peoples, and how his account contributes to the history of Mizoram. Confirm specific incidents from the chapters themselves.

The work records Guevara's youthful journey through Latin America. Encounters with poverty, illness and inequality gradually broaden the journey from personal adventure into social and political awakening.

In 1952, 23-year-old medical student Ernesto Guevara and his friend Alberto Granado travelled about 8,000 km across South America - Argentina, Chile, Peru, Colombia and Venezuela - on an old Norton motorcycle called 'La Poderosa' (The Mighty One), which eventually broke down.

Along the way he met poor miners in Chile (including a communist couple), indigenous people in Peru and patients at the San Pablo leper colony in the Amazon, where he swam across the river to be with the patients. These experiences awakened his belief in a united Latin America and social justice, later leading to his role in the Cuban Revolution.

sections.title: Travel Writing as a Literary Form

blocks.text:
Travel writing is more than a factual record of movement from one place to another. It presents places through the traveller's perspective and may include history, politics, culture, personal experience and encounters with other communities.

The syllabus uses Tim Youngs's introduction to establish this background. Travel writing can shape ideas of self and other, and it must therefore be read critically: who is travelling, who is being described, and what historical or political position influences the description?
Nature: Travel writing is a first-person, mostly factual account of journeys that combines description of places with the traveller's experiences, reflections, history and culture.

Critical reading: Following Tim Youngs and postcolonial critics, readers should ask who travels, with what power and purpose, how other cultures are represented, and whose voices are silenced. Travel writing has often supported colonial views but can also challenge them.

Prescribed texts: Ghosh shows travel as historical inquiry; Lewin represents the colonial administrator-traveller; Guevara shows travel as political awakening. Together they illustrate the range of the genre.

Amitav Ghosh's Dancing in Cambodia uses travel writing to connect place with history and memory. Cambodia is presented not merely as a destination but as a society marked by political violence and cultural survival.

Ghosh's approach shows how travel writing can combine observation, historical inquiry and reflection. Culture and performance become ways of thinking about what survives after political destruction.

Content: Ghosh links King Sisowath's 1906 journey with his royal dancers to the Colonial Exhibition in Marseilles - where they were admired as exotic spectacle - with his own visit to Cambodia after the Khmer Rouge genocide, during which dancers and artists were killed.

Themes: Colonialism and the European gaze, the fragility and survival of culture, the violence of history, memory and identity. The revival of classical dance by surviving artists symbolises resilience.
Technique: Ghosh blends travelogue, history, reportage and reflection, moving between past and present. The essay shows how travel writing can go beyond sightseeing to understand societies.

The syllabus prescribes Chapters IX, X and XI from Lt. Col. Thomas Lewin's A Fly on the Wheel or How I Helped to Govern India. The work belongs to a colonial historical context and should be studied both for the places and people described and for the viewpoint of the British administrator-traveller.

Because the uploaded syllabus does not reproduce these chapters, detailed incidents and quotations should be learned from the prescribed selections.

Author and context: Lewin was a British officer in the Chittagong Hill Tracts who took part in the Lushai Expedition (1871-72) and became known among the Mizos as 'Thangliana'. His memoir records his life as an administrator among the hill tribes.

Reading the chapters: Students should note the places, people, customs and events described in Chapters IX-XI and examine how Lewin presents the hill peoples - with sympathy, curiosity or colonial superiority.

Significance: The work is a valuable historical source on early contact between the British and the Mizos, but it reflects a colonial perspective. Critical reading should balance its information with awareness of whose viewpoint it represents.

The Motorcycle Diaries records the journey of the young Ernesto 'Che' Guevara across Latin America. The journey begins with adventure and discovery, but encounters with poverty, disease and social inequality gradually change his understanding of the continent.

The work therefore combines travel, autobiography and political awakening. Landscape and movement are important, but the human encounters become central to Guevara's developing social consciousness.

Journey: In 1952 Ernesto Guevara and Alberto Granado set out from Buenos Aires on 'La Poderosa', travelling through Chile, Peru, Colombia and Venezuela, often hitchhiking after the motorcycle broke down.

Transformation: Meetings with exploited miners at Chuquicamata, indigenous people in the Andes, and lepers at San Pablo made Guevara aware of poverty, injustice and the shared identity of Latin America. On his birthday at San Pablo he toasted a united Latin America.

Significance: The diaries combine youthful adventure, humour, travel description and political awakening. They show how travel can change a person's worldview and help explain Guevara's later revolutionary life.

sections.title: ENG 204 – WRITINGS FROM NORTH EAST INDIA
SHORT NOTES
context: ENG 204 – WRITINGS FROM NORTH EAST INDIA

sections.title: Background – Tilottoma Misra
context: ENG 204 – WRITINGS FROM NORTH EAST INDIA

blocks.text: The prescribed introduction to The Oxford Anthology of Writings from North-East India provides a background for reading the region's literature in relation to its diverse peoples, histories, cultures and political experiences.

Tilottoma Misra edited 'The Oxford Anthology of Writings from North-East India' (2011) in two volumes (poetry and essays; fiction). Her introduction explains that the North-East is home to many ethnic groups, languages and cultures with strong oral traditions, and that its literature reflects histories of colonialism, migration, insurgency, identity politics and ecological change.

She stresses that the region should not be seen as one homogeneous entity and that writing from the North-East - in English and in translation - gives voice to experiences often ignored by mainstream Indian literature.

sections.title: O Poor Hachukrai – Chandrakanta Murasingh
context: ENG 204 – WRITINGS FROM NORTH EAST INDIA

blocks.text: A prescribed poem from Tripura. Students should study its voice, imagery, themes and regional cultural context from the assigned text.
Chandrakanta Murasingh is a well-known Kokborok poet from Tripura. Hachukrai refers to the hills and hill-dwelling people of Tripura in the Kokborok language.

When studying, focus on the speaker's address to Hachukrai, images of hill life and nature, and concerns that may include poverty, displacement and changing tribal life, as found in the prescribed poem.

sections.title: A Himalayan Ballad – Guru T. Ladakhi
context: ENG 204 – WRITINGS FROM NORTH EAST INDIA

blocks.text: A prescribed poem from Sikkim. It should be read for its poetic treatment of Himalayan life, setting and regional experience.
Guru T. Ladakhi is a poet from Sikkim who writes in English. The ballad form suggests a story-like poem, often with repetition and simple rhythm.
Study the poem's Himalayan setting, the life of mountain people, any narrative it contains and its themes, which may include tradition, change and the landscape's influence on people.

sections.title: Sundori – Kynpham S. Nongkynrih
context: ENG 204 – WRITINGS FROM NORTH EAST INDIA

blocks.text: A prescribed poem from Meghalaya. Students should focus on speaker, imagery, cultural setting and central concerns in the assigned poem.
Kynpham Sing Nongkynrih is a Khasi poet from Shillong, Meghalaya, who writes in Khasi and English and co-edited anthologies of North-East poetry with Robin Ngangom.
Study who Sundori is in the poem, the speaker's attitude toward her, the imagery and the social or cultural issues (such as gender, class or community) raised in the text.

sections.title: We Are Not Ready for the Hand of Peace – Robin S. Ngangom
context: ENG 204 – WRITINGS FROM NORTH EAST INDIA

blocks.text: A prescribed poem from Manipur whose title itself places peace and conflict at the centre. Detailed interpretation should remain tied to the assigned text.

Robin S. Ngangom is a Manipuri poet writing in English and Meitei, known for poems about violence and insurgency in Manipur. His work often contrasts the beauty of the land with the brutality of conflict.
Study how the poem presents violence, fear and the difficulty of accepting peace after long conflict, its tone (bitter, ironic) and its imagery.

sections.title: The Voice of the Mountain – Mamang Dai
context: ENG 204 – WRITINGS FROM NORTH EAST INDIA

blocks.text: A prescribed poem from Arunachal Pradesh. It should be studied for its representation of landscape, voice, memory and the relationship between people and place.
Mamang Dai is a poet, novelist and former journalist from Arunachal Pradesh (Adi community), awarded the Padma Shri. Her poems often draw on Adi myths, rivers, mountains and oral traditions.
In this poem, consider the mountain as a speaking voice, its connection to memory, origins and the spirit world, and the relationship between people and land.

sections.title: Chhingpuii – Kaphleia
context: ENG 204 – WRITINGS FROM NORTH EAST INDIA

blocks.text: A prescribed prose text from Mizoram. Students should study the narrative, characters, setting, themes and cultural significance from the assigned text.
Kaphleia (1910-1940) was a pioneering Mizo poet and writer. 'Chhingpuii' draws on the Mizo tradition of tragic love stories.

Study the narrative and characters from the prescribed text, the setting in traditional Mizo village life, the themes of love, loss and fate, and the story's place in Mizo literary and oral tradition.

sections.title: Parasu's Well – Indira Goswami
context: ENG 204 – WRITINGS FROM NORTH EAST INDIA

blocks.text: A prescribed prose text from Assam. Students should prepare its plot, characters, social setting and central concerns from the assigned reading.

Indira Goswami (Mamoni Raisom Goswami, 1942-2011) was an Assamese writer who won the Jnanpith Award (2000). Her fiction often deals with the oppression of women, widows and the poor, and social hypocrisy.
Prepare the plot of 'Parasu's Well' from the text, the main characters, the social setting and the central concerns, linking them to her wider themes.

sections.title: When the River Sleeps – Easterine Kire
context: ENG 204 – WRITINGS FROM NORTH EAST INDIA

blocks.text: The novel follows Vilie, a hunter who undertakes a dangerous journey connected with a mysterious stone and the sleeping river. The work combines Naga cultural beliefs, nature, spirituality, adventure and the individual's relationship with the unseen world.

Easterine Kire is a Naga writer; 'When the River Sleeps' (2014) won the Hindu Literary Prize. Vilie lives alone in the forest guarding it from poachers. He dreams of a river that sleeps once a year, when a person can take a heart-stone from its bed that gives special power.

His journey takes him through dangerous forests with spirits, weretigers and the 'unclean forest', and he meets people, including women with spiritual powers, who help or threaten him. Themes: Naga oral tradition and animist beliefs, the spirit world, nature, courage, solitude and the meaning of power. Confirm details from the text.

sections.title: LONG NOTES
context: ENG 204 – WRITINGS FROM NORTH EAST INDIA

sections.title: Background to Writings from North East India
context: ENG 204 – WRITINGS FROM NORTH EAST INDIA

blocks.text:
The course introduces writings in English from India's North-Eastern region. According to the syllabus, its purpose is to help students understand the heterogeneous social, political, cultural and historical conditions from which these writings arise.

Tilottoma Misra's prescribed introduction provides the background. Students should avoid treating the North East as a single culture; the paper deliberately includes writers from Tripura, Sikkim, Meghalaya, Manipur, Arunachal Pradesh, Mizoram, Assam and Nagaland.

Diversity of the region: The North-East includes eight states with hundreds of communities, languages and religions. Its literature, often rooted in oral traditions, myths and folk songs, reflects this diversity.

Historical and political background: Colonial rule, Partition, migration, ethnic conflict, insurgency, militarisation (e.g. AFSPA), development and ecological change shape the writing. Writers express identity, loss, violence, memory and the relationship with land.

Misra's introduction: It warns against seeing the region as exotic or homogeneous and places its writing within Indian and world literature. The course includes writers from Tripura, Sikkim, Meghalaya, Manipur, Arunachal Pradesh, Mizoram, Assam and Nagaland to show this plurality.

sections.title: Poetry from North East India
context: ENG 204 – WRITINGS FROM NORTH EAST INDIA

blocks.text:
The prescribed poets are Chandrakanta Murasingh, Guru T. Ladakhi, Kynpham S. Nongkynrih, Robin S. Ngangom and Mamang Dai. Their poems represent different states and literary voices.

For long answers, students should compare the treatment of place, identity, culture, memory, conflict and nature only where these features are present in the actual poems. The syllabus provides titles and regional identification but does not reproduce the poems, so close textual details must come from the prescribed anthologies.
Poets: Chandrakanta Murasingh (Tripura, Kokborok), Guru T. Ladakhi (Sikkim), Kynpham S. Nongkynrih (Meghalaya, Khasi), Robin S. Ngangom (Manipur) and Mamang Dai (Arunachal Pradesh, Adi).

Common concerns: Many poets from the region write about land and landscape, oral tradition and myth, identity and marginalisation, violence and conflict, and changes in tribal life. Ngangom's poem directly addresses conflict and peace; Dai's poem gives voice to the mountain and memory.
Answer writing: Compare poems on themes like place, identity, culture and conflict using lines from the prescribed texts, and note differences in tone and style.

sections.title: Chhingpuii and Parasu's Well
context: ENG 204 – WRITINGS FROM NORTH EAST INDIA

blocks.text:
Kaphleia's 'Chhingpuii' represents Mizoram and Indira Goswami's 'Parasu's Well' represents Assam in the syllabus. Both should be prepared through plot, character, setting, social or cultural context and central themes.

The uploaded syllabus does not include the full stories. Therefore, detailed incidents should be taken from the prescribed texts rather than reconstructed from unsupported summaries.

Kaphleia's 'Chhingpuii': A Mizo text rooted in traditional village life and tragic love, important in the history of Mizo literature. Study plot, characters, cultural setting and themes from the prescribed text.

Indira Goswami's 'Parasu's Well': An Assamese story by a Jnanpith-winning writer known for depicting social injustice and the suffering of the marginalised. Prepare plot, characters and social concerns from the text.
Comparison: Both texts show how regional literature reflects local society and values; compare their settings, characters and themes using details from the actual stories.

sections.title: When the River Sleeps
context: ENG 204 – WRITINGS FROM NORTH EAST INDIA

blocks.text:
Easterine Kire's When the River Sleeps is set within a Naga cultural and natural world. Vilie's journey toward the sleeping river develops as both an adventure and a spiritual encounter.

The novel gives importance to landscape, traditional beliefs and the relationship between visible and unseen realities. The journey structure allows the novel to explore courage, solitude, community, nature and indigenous cultural knowledge.

Plot: Vilie, a solitary hunter, sets out to find the sleeping river and its heart-stone. His journey through forests full of spirits, weretigers and dangers tests his courage and wisdom; he obtains the stone, faces those who want it and eventually understands its true meaning.

Themes: The Naga worldview in which the natural and spirit worlds are connected, respect for nature, courage and solitude, the dangers of greed and power, and the importance of oral tradition and indigenous knowledge.

Style: Kire blends folklore, myth and realism (magical realism), with a simple narrative voice and rich descriptions of landscape. The novel presents Naga culture from within, challenging outsiders' stereotypes.
The main parts of speech are noun, pronoun, adjective, verb, adverb, preposition, conjunction and interjection. Understanding their functions helps students construct grammatically correct sentences.

Functions: a noun names (Mizoram, book, honesty); a pronoun replaces a noun (he, it, they); an adjective describes a noun (tall, three); a verb shows action or state (run, is); an adverb modifies a verb, adjective or adverb (quickly, very); a preposition shows relation (in, on, under); a conjunction joins (and, but, because); an interjection expresses emotion (Oh! Alas!).
The same word can belong to different parts of speech depending on use: 'He runs fast' (adverb) vs 'They fast on Sundays' (verb).

Tense shows the time and state of an action or situation. English commonly organises tense forms around present, past and future reference, with simple, continuous, perfect and perfect continuous forms.

Twelve tense forms: Present - simple (I write), continuous (I am writing), perfect (I have written), perfect continuous (I have been writing); Past - wrote, was writing, had written, had been writing; Future - will write, will be writing, will have written, will have been writing.

Uses: simple present for habits and facts ('The sun rises in the east'); present perfect for past actions with present relevance ('I have finished'); past perfect for the earlier of two past actions ('The train had left before I arrived').
Active voice places the doer as subject, while passive voice places emphasis on the receiver of the action. Example: 'The student wrote the answer' becomes 'The answer was written by the student.'

Rules: the object of the active becomes the subject of the passive; the verb takes 'be' + past participle according to tense ('writes' - 'is written'; 'wrote' - 'was written'; 'is writing' - 'is being written'; 'has written' - 'has been written'; 'will write' - 'will be written'); the subject becomes 'by + agent', which may be omitted.
Passive is used when the doer is unknown or unimportant ('The road was repaired') and in formal writing. Imperatives: 'Shut the door' - 'Let the door be shut'.
Direct speech gives the speaker's exact words. Indirect speech reports the meaning with necessary changes in pronouns, tense, time expressions and sentence structure.

Rules: if the reporting verb is in the past, present tenses change to past ('is' - 'was', 'will' - 'would', 'has' - 'had'); pronouns change according to the speaker; 'now' becomes 'then', 'today' - 'that day', 'tomorrow' - 'the next day', 'here' - 'there', 'this' - 'that'.

Questions use 'asked' with 'if/whether' or the question word: He said, 'Are you ready?' - He asked if I was ready. Commands use 'told/ordered' + to-infinitive: She said, 'Sit down' - She told me to sit down. Universal truths do not change tense.
Concord means grammatical agreement, especially between subject and verb. A singular subject generally takes a singular verb and a plural subject a plural verb, subject to specific rules.

Rules: two subjects joined by 'and' take a plural verb ('Ram and Shyam are friends'); with 'either...or', 'neither...nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject; words like 'each', 'every', 'everyone', 'nobody' take singular verbs; 'The number of' takes singular, 'A number of' takes plural; collective nouns take singular when acting as a unit ('The committee has decided').
Words joined by 'with', 'along with', 'as well as' do not change the number of the subject ('The teacher, with her students, is coming').
An idiom is an expression whose meaning cannot always be understood literally. Knowledge of common idioms improves comprehension and effective language use.

Examples: 'a piece of cake' (very easy), 'to burn the midnight oil' (to study late at night), 'to let the cat out of the bag' (to reveal a secret), 'to bite the dust' (to be defeated), 'once in a blue moon' (rarely), 'to hit the nail on the head' (to say exactly the right thing), 'a blessing in disguise', 'to break the ice'.
Phrasal verbs such as 'give up', 'look after', 'put off' and 'carry out' are also important. Use idioms in correct contexts and learn them through reading.
Expansion develops a short statement, idea or proverb into a clear paragraph by explaining its meaning, giving reasons and adding relevant examples.

Steps: understand the central idea; write an opening sentence that explains it; give reasons, illustrations and examples (from history, daily life or literature); show different aspects or contrasts; and conclude by restating the idea's significance. Length is usually 150-250 words.
Example: expanding 'Honesty is the best policy' - explain honesty, show its long-term rewards (trust, respect), contrast with the temporary gains of dishonesty, give an example, and conclude.
Comprehension tests the ability to understand a passage, identify main ideas, locate information, infer meaning and answer accurately from the text.

Strategy: skim the passage for the general idea, read the questions, then read the passage carefully and locate answers. Answer in your own words where possible, keep answers brief and relevant, and do not add outside information.
Question types include factual questions, inference questions, vocabulary in context, finding the main idea or a suitable title, and identifying the author's tone or purpose.
A précis is a concise and accurate restatement of a passage in one's own words. It keeps the main ideas while removing repetition and unnecessary detail.

Rules: a précis is usually one-third of the original length; it should have a title; it is written in the third person and in reported speech; it omits examples, repetitions, figures of speech and minor details; it must not add new ideas or personal opinions.

Steps: read the passage several times, identify main ideas, make a rough draft, compare it with the original for accuracy, revise for length and coherence, and write the fair copy with a suitable title.
An essay presents organised ideas on a topic. A good essay normally has an introduction, logically arranged body paragraphs and a conclusion.

Types: descriptive, narrative, expository, argumentative and reflective essays. Steps: understand the topic, brainstorm ideas, prepare an outline, write the introduction (hook and thesis), body paragraphs (each with one main idea, supporting details and examples) and conclusion (summary and final thought).
Qualities of a good essay: unity, coherence (with linking words), clarity, relevance, correct grammar, variety of sentences and a balanced length.

sections.title: Parts of Speech, Tense and Voice

blocks.text:
Parts of speech classify words according to their grammatical functions. Correct identification of nouns, pronouns, adjectives, verbs, adverbs, prepositions, conjunctions and interjections helps students understand sentence structure.

Tense expresses time and aspect of actions. Voice changes the focus of a sentence between the doer and receiver of an action. Practice should include identifying forms and transforming sentences without changing the essential meaning.
Parts of speech: Knowing the eight parts of speech and their functions helps in analysing sentences and avoiding errors. A word's part of speech depends on its use in a sentence.

Tense: English has present, past and future time, each with simple, continuous, perfect and perfect continuous forms. Correct use of tense shows when an action happens and whether it is complete or ongoing.

Voice: Active voice emphasises the doer; passive voice emphasises the action or receiver. Conversion requires changing the object to subject, using 'be' + past participle according to tense, and adding 'by + agent' when needed. Practice with transformation exercises builds accuracy.

sections.title: Direct and Indirect Speech, Concord and Idioms

blocks.text:
Direct speech records exact words, whereas indirect speech reports what was said. Conversion requires attention to reporting verbs, pronouns, tense and expressions of time and place.

Concord mainly concerns grammatical agreement between subject and verb. Idioms and phrases require familiarity because their meanings may not be literal. These areas are especially useful for correct writing and competitive examinations.

Direct and indirect speech: Conversion requires changing reporting verbs (said to - told, asked), pronouns, tenses (backshift), and time and place words, and using suitable connectives for questions (if, whether, wh-words) and commands (to-infinitive).
Concord: Subject and verb must agree in number and person. Special rules apply to compound subjects, 'either/neither', indefinite pronouns, collective nouns and phrases like 'as well as'.
Idioms and phrases: Idioms have figurative meanings and make language lively. Learning common idioms and phrasal verbs improves comprehension, writing and performance in competitive examinations.

Comprehension requires careful reading. Students should identify the main idea, distinguish major points from details and answer only from what the passage supports.

Précis writing reduces a passage to its essential meaning. A good précis is clear, concise, logically connected and written mainly in the student's own words without adding personal opinion.

Comprehension: Read actively - skim, then scan for details. Identify the main idea, supporting points, the author's purpose and tone, and infer meanings of unfamiliar words from context. Answer precisely from the passage.
Précis writing: Reduce the passage to about one-third, keeping all essential ideas in a logical order, using one's own words, third person and past tense where appropriate, with a suitable title.
Skills developed: Both exercises develop careful reading, analysis, summarising and clear expression, which are valuable in academic study and professional life.

Expansion of a passage or idea requires explaining its meaning in a developed and connected form. Relevant reasons, illustrations and examples can be added without moving away from the central idea.

Essay writing requires a clear introduction, organised body and conclusion. Students should maintain relevance, paragraph unity, grammatical accuracy and logical sequence throughout.
Expansion: Develop the idea by explaining its meaning, giving reasons and examples, and concluding with its relevance, without drifting from the central theme.

Essay writing: Plan with an outline, write an engaging introduction with a clear thesis, develop body paragraphs each with a topic sentence and support, use linking words for coherence, and write a conclusion that summarises and reflects.
Common mistakes to avoid: irrelevance, repetition, very long paragraphs, grammatical errors and lack of examples. Revising the draft improves quality.
